title: Third-party C2 app assurance and onboarding pipeline (continuous security assessment, RBAC/audit-logging conformance, SBOM, accreditation-as-code) for NGC2, TAK, Overmatch Armory and the Jailbreak API marketplace
problem: The Army wants an open C2 app ecosystem, but its flagship NGC2 prototype hosted third-party apps that had never been assessed (25 to 200+ vulnerabilities each) with no access control or user-activity logging, and every ecosystem (NGC2 team leads, TAK third-party pipeline, Overmatch Software Armory, the new API marketplace) re-invents app onboarding and evidence generation by hand.
echelons: division/corps program level (NGC2 team leads, PM C2 Applications)
enterprise (Army CIO/CTO authorizing official, TAK Product Center, NAVWAR)

user.exact_role: NGC2 team-lead integration/DevSecOps engineers; PM C2 Applications pipeline staff; TAK Product Center third-party pipeline operators; Overmatch Software Armory platform staff; Army CIO/CTO authorizing official and program-office ISSMs; engineers at small vendors trying to get an app accepted
user.echelon: Program office / enterprise (not a tactical operator problem)
organization_examples: CPE C2IN (ex-PEO C3N), PM C2 Applications
Army CIO / Office of the CTO (authorizing official for the NGC2 prototype)
Team Anduril / Team Lockheed NGC2 integrators and their sub-vendors (Raft, Rune, RII, Govini, Striveworks)
NAVWAR / NIWC Pacific Overmatch Software Armory

current_workflow: 1. Vendor builds an app against the ecosystem SDK (Lattice SDK / Foundry, ATAK plugin SDK, Armory container baseline).
2. Vendor submits source or binary to the team lead (NGC2), the TAK third-party build/sign service (tak.gov/user_builds), or the Armory RAISE pipeline.

3. Ecosystem runs its own checks: TAK pipeline builds and signs and marks third-party plugins in the UI; Armory applies RAISE requirements; NGC2 team leads did ad hoc internal review during the 2025 prototype.
4. App is deployed into the prototype/exercise environment (Ivy Sting, Lightning Surge, PC-C6).
5. Government assessment happens after the fact: the Army CTO/AO assessment (Sept 2025) found unassessed third-party apps, no RBAC and no user-activity logging.
6. Remediation and re-deployment; Army CIO says issues were triaged and mitigated (Oct 2025).
7. Every new ecosystem or new version repeats the process; the Army is now (May 2026 RFI) trying to buy a standard storefront and DevSecOps pipeline to stop repeating it.
current_solution: TAK Product Center third-party pipeline (ephemeral build + sign, third-party visual indicator; earlier stage evidence cites OWASP dependency-check and Fortify SAST); Overmatch Software Armory as a RAISE Platform of Choice (containerized apps inherit the production ATO); Platform One Iron Bank / Big Bang hardened containers; Second Front Game Warden ATO-inheritance hosting; Defense Unicorns UDS (Zarf, UDS Registry, Lula compliance-as-code); Anchore/Chainguard SBOM and hardened images; RegScale/Paramify OSCAL-based compliance automation; team-lead internal reviews inside NGC2; DoD CIO SWFT (third-party assessment + vendor and third-party SBOM for provisional ATO).
failure: Checks are per-ecosystem, binary/container-level and after-the-fact. Nothing in the existing toolchain verifies that an app enforces role/attribute-based access inside its own data model, emits standardized audit events an AO can see across apps from different vendors, or carries evidence in a form reusable across NGC2, TAK, Armory and the API marketplace. The Sept 2025 memo failure ('we cannot control who sees what, we cannot see what users are doing, and we cannot verify that the software itself is secure') is an application-layer conformance failure that container scanning and SBOMs do not catch.

evidence.claim: Army CTO/authorizing official memo (signed Sept 5 2025) rated the NGC2 prototype 'very high risk': any authorized user could reach all applications and data regardless of need, no logging of user actions, and hosted third-party apps had not undergone Army security assessment (one with 25 high-severity vulnerabilities, others waiting for checks).
evidence.source_title: Anduril and Palantir battlefield communication system 'very high risk,' US Army memo says (CNBC/Reuters)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: The memo lists 'unverified and vulnerable codebase for third-party applications' and 'lack of access control and accountability' as critical deficiencies; Anduril called it an outdated snapshot and Palantir said no vulnerabilities were found in its platform, i.e. the failure sat in the third-party app layer and platform governance, not the data platform.
evidence.source_title: Move Fast, But Don't Break the Battlefield (The Defense Circuit) and CNBC company responses
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: ACC-APG issued Special Notice C2APPSRFI-1, 'Request for Information - Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) Software Application Storefront, Pipeline and Tailorable Warfighting Applications', posted 2026-05-12 with responses due 2026-05-27 - the Army is actively surveying industry for the app storefront and onboarding pipeline.
evidence.source_title: NGC2 Software Application Storefront, Pipeline and Tailorable Warfighting Applications RFI (HigherGov mirror of SAM.gov notice)
evidence.label: FACT (notice existence and dates from search summary; full text not retrieved - domain blocked)

evidence.claim: PM C2 Applications (Dennis Teefy) says it will enable third-party integration of applications into the NGC2 ecosystem, that commercial industry can build its own DevSecOps pipeline to bring in third-party apps for the eventual application store, and that pipeline establishment must precede the storefront.
evidence.source_title: DoD Modernization Exchange 2026: Army's Dennis Teefy on building application layer for NGC2 (Federal News Network)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: DoD CIO Software Fast Track (SWFT) memo (April 24 2025; live June 1 2025) requires vendor SBOM plus a third-party-assessor SBOM and a third-party assessment on 12 risk factors, with AI-assisted back-end review leading to a provisional ATO - a department-wide mandate that makes machine-readable app assurance evidence a gating item.
evidence.source_title: Inside the Pentagon CIO's push to overhaul antiquated software acquisition practices (DefenseScoop)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: TAK.gov runs an ephemeral third-party build-and-sign service (submissions at tak.gov/user_builds, ~20 min review, third-party visual indicator in the app) open to anyone not on the Denied Parties List - one ecosystem's own onboarding pipeline that covers signing but not in-app access-control or audit conformance.
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Overmatch Software Armory earned RAISE Platform of Choice designation: containerized CI/CD apps that meet RAISE requirements are incorporated into the production ATO without a separate authorization - a second, Navy-specific onboarding pipeline.
evidence.source_title: RAISE 2.0 and Overmatch Software Armory (DON CIO)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Defense Unicorns' Lula ingests OSCAL, validates NIST 800-53 controls against a live environment and uploads findings to RegScale; RegScale open-sourced an OSCAL Hub (Dec 2025); Defense Unicorns raised $136M Series B (Jan 2026) and launched UDS Registry - compliance-as-code for the platform/container layer is already served by well-capitalized vendors.
evidence.source_title: defenseunicorns/lula (GitHub); RegScale Open Sources OSCAL Hub (Security Boulevard); Defense Unicorns $136M Series B (GovConWire)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: DoD CIO 'State of DevSecOps' (March 2025): authorizing officials are 'biased to caution' and reciprocity is lacking or unclear - explains why each ecosystem re-runs its own checks instead of accepting another's evidence.
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Operation Jailbreak (Fort Carson, May 2026, ~78 vendors given API access) produced an Army API Marketplace overseen by the Army Data Operations Center, and the Army says documented APIs/MOSA will be prerequisites in future contracts - a third onboarding surface with its own vetting needs.
evidence.source_title: From the Army Acquisition Executive: The Right to Integrate (army.mil); Army pilot data ops center to oversee Pentagon's first API marketplace (Inside Defense)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: GAO-26-108019 (Aug 20 2026): Army lacks a detailed NGC2 fielding schedule and life-cycle cost estimate for scaling to all units by FY2032; ~$3.3B identified through FY2026. Scaling from two prototype divisions to 11 divisions and 4 corps implies app acceptance must become repeatable rather than bespoke.
evidence.source_title: Army Modernization: Better Schedule and Cost Information Needed to Support Scaling Battlefield Network (GAO-26-108019)
evidence.label: INFERENCE

evidence.claim: Anduril reported 65+ edge nodes and 20+ applications at Ivy Sting 5, setting the onboarding volume per exercise (vendor account; not independently verified).
evidence.source_title: Scaling Next Generation Command and Control from prototype to fight (Anduril)
evidence.label: FACT (company-reported)

why_existing_startups_havent_solved: The DevSecOps vendors (Second Front, Defense Unicorns, Rise8, Anchore, Chainguard) solve hosting, container hardening, SBOM and control inheritance for the platform; GRC vendors (RegScale, Paramify) solve evidence assembly for the ATO package; platform owners (Anduril Lattice, Palantir Apollo/Foundry) control their own app models. None of them sells application-behaviour conformance - proof that a third-party app enforces role/attribute-based access on the data it renders and emits standardized, AO-visible audit events - because until the Sept 2025 memo no buyer had articulated that requirement, and because the requirement owner (Army CIO/CTO as AO) and the pipeline owner (PM C2 Applications) are different offices from the app buyers (team leads). The May 2026 RFI shows the Army now intends to buy a storefront and pipeline itself, which will most likely go to an integrator or an existing DevSecOps vendor, leaving a startup the in-app conformance niche at best.
technical_wedge: An 'app conformance kit': (a) an open-source policy/audit SDK for Lattice-SDK apps, ATAK plugins and Armory containers that wires attribute-based access decisions and structured audit events (OpenTelemetry/OCSF-style) into the app with a few lines of code; (b) a conformance tester that drives the app with synthetic users/roles and synthetic tagged data and produces a machine-readable report proving need-to-know enforcement, audit completeness and SBOM/provenance, expressed as OSCAL assessment results consumable by Lula/RegScale, the TAK pipeline, RAISE and the future NGC2 storefront pipeline; (c) an AO dashboard that aggregates those events across apps from different vendors. The wedge is app-layer behaviour, not container scanning, which is already commoditized.

mvp.what: Open-source SDK + conformance tester for ATAK-CIV plugins and a Lattice-SDK sample app; publishes a signed OSCAL assessment-results bundle (RBAC test matrix, audit-event coverage, SBOM) and a small cross-app audit viewer.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Two existing open-source ATAK plugins and one Lattice-SDK sandbox app instrumented and tested end-to-end on commercial hardware; a live demo where a 'user without need-to-know' is denied and the denial appears in the AO viewer; output bundle ingested by Lula and by a mock TAK/Armory pipeline; one NGC2 sub-vendor pilot or TPC feedback letter.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That an app can be made to pass the exact failures in the Sept 2025 memo (who-sees-what, what-users-did, is-the-code-vetted) with days not months of vendor effort, and that at least one pipeline owner (PM C2 Applications, TPC or Armory) will accept the evidence format instead of re-testing.

data_requirement.what: No operational data needed for MVP; needs ecosystem interface specs (Lattice SDK docs, ATAK plugin SDK, Armory/RAISE requirements, Iron Bank hardening guides), NIST 800-53/RMF control mappings, OSCAL schemas, and eventually the NGC2 storefront pipeline submission format (likely CUI).
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: Yes for MVP: Lattice SDK docs and sandbox are available to developers, ATAK-CIV and the TAK third-party pipeline are open to anyone not on the Denied Parties List, RAISE guidance and cATO evaluation criteria are public DoD CIO documents. NGC2-specific pipeline specs will require being on a team or an RFI response and are likely CUI with need-to-know restrictions.

entry_vehicle.primary: Sell the open-source conformance kit and paid support to NGC2 sub-vendors and team leads, then respond as a component to the NGC2 storefront/pipeline effort (C2APPSRFI-1 successor solicitation) as a subcontractor to whoever wins the pipeline.

entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR requires the small business to be >50% owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (or by other qualifying small businesses); an Indonesian founder who is not a U.S. person holding a large equity stake may make the company ineligible or require capitalization restructuring - needs counsel. Non-SBIR routes (OTA subcontract, commercial sale to team leads, xTech prize eligibility) have different rules. The software itself is likely EAR-controlled at most (commercial security tooling), but NGC2 pipeline specifications are probably CUI with need-to-know and possibly U.S.-person-only access under the prime's flow-downs; TAK third-party pipeline is explicitly open to anyone not on the Denied Parties List. Do not assume; verify with export-control and government-contracts counsel.

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes, easily. Anduril and Palantir control the SDKs and were publicly embarrassed by the memo; adding attribute-based access enforcement and audit hooks to the Lattice SDK / Foundry app model is the obvious fix and Anduril already says the memo is an 'outdated snapshot'. PM C2 Applications is procuring the pipeline itself, and Defense Unicorns/Second Front can extend existing products to app-level checks.
incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: Partial reject as a standalone company. The only defensible position is ecosystem-neutral conformance evidence that an AO trusts across Anduril, Palantir, TAK and Navy pipelines - something no platform owner is incentivized to build for its competitors. That neutrality is real but small, it depends on an AO choosing to require it, and it is most plausibly a feature of the winning pipeline vendor or an open-source standard rather than a venture-scale product.

expertise_required.why: Builds the conformance tester and SDK; must be credible to Anchore/Chainguard-class reviewers.

SBIR ownership rules, CUI flow-downs and non-U.S.-person founder structure must be resolved before revenue.

regulatory_burden.explanation: MVP is unclassified, uses open SDKs and public standards. Production work requires handling CUI (pipeline specs, assessment results), DFARS 252.204-7012 / CMMC Level 2 readiness, and AO acceptance of the evidence format; no ITAR-controlled technical data is inherent to the product, but ecosystem specs may carry distribution restrictions. Not legal advice; needs counsel.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: An Indonesian founder who is not a U.S. person: (1) may affect SBIR/STTR ownership eligibility (>50% U.S. citizen/permanent-resident ownership and control); (2) may be excluded from CUI/need-to-know data under prime flow-downs and from facility/secret clearances later; (3) FOCI mitigation could be triggered if foreign ownership or control is significant and the company pursues cleared work. The TAK third-party pipeline itself is open to non-U.S. persons not on the Denied Parties List. Describe, structure, and confirm with counsel; no definitive judgment here.

dual_use_potential.explanation: App-level RBAC/audit conformance testing and OSCAL evidence generation map to FedRAMP, healthcare and financial app marketplaces and to any enterprise 'internal app store' with compliance gates; the SDK integrations (ATAK/Lattice) are defense-specific but the tester and evidence format are not. Commercial buyers, however, already have mature AppSec/GRC vendors, so the dual-use path is a crowded one.

defensibility.explanation: Defensibility would come from an AO-accepted evidence format (de facto standard) and from being wired into several ecosystems' submission pipelines. Neither is patentable and both can be replicated by the platform owner or the pipeline winner; the open-source route gives adoption but weakens capture. Realistic defensibility: low.

why_now: Three changes since 2023: (1) the Sept 2025 Army CTO memo made third-party app assurance, need-to-know enforcement and user-activity logging an explicit, public gating requirement for NGC2; (2) DoD CIO SWFT (Apr-Jun 2025) and the Jan 2026 DoD AI strategy memo mandate machine-readable SBOM/third-party assessment and a 'wartime' push to remove ATO blockers; (3) the Army is now buying the ecosystem plumbing - PM C2 Applications stood up (Dec 2025 reorg), the storefront/pipeline RFI (May 2026), the API Marketplace (May 2026) and the common data baseline (June 2026) - so the onboarding surface is being standardized right now and the format will be set in the next 12-18 months.
killer_risk: The Army is procuring the storefront and DevSecOps pipeline itself (C2APPSRFI-1, PM C2 Applications), and the platform owners (Anduril, Palantir) and well-capitalized DevSecOps/GRC vendors (Defense Unicorns, Second Front, Anchore, Chainguard, RegScale) already cover every layer except in-app behaviour conformance, which they can add as a feature. There is no commercial buyer for a neutral third-party assurance product unless an AO mandates it, and an AO is more likely to mandate government or pipeline-winner tooling than a two-person startup's format.

allied_extension: Somewhat more compelling with allies, but not enough to change the verdict. TAK is used across NATO and the TAK third-party pipeline is open to non-U.S. developers; Project Overmatch has a Five Eyes agreement; the Army says Jailbreak will extend to foreign partners; and allied ecosystems (Bundeswehr, NATO DIANA channels open to the German founder) face the same app-vetting problem with even less tooling. But each ally has its own accreditation authority and reciprocity is weaker across nations than across U.S. services, so the 'one evidence format' thesis gets harder, not easier, and allied programs are smaller. A German/NATO-first variant is a plausible optionality play, not a stronger core.
